opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Voice is one of the most latency-sensitive applications you can build on top of a language model. In a text chat, if the model takes a second or two to respond, people tolerate it. In a spoken conversation, a long pause feels unnatural. People expect a reply within a few hundred milliseconds, roughly the way another person would respond. So the whole pipeline has to be fast: speech recognition, the language model, and text-to-speech. The language model is very often the bottleneck.

That's where diffusion language models have a structural advantage. Traditional autoregressive models generate one token at a time, left to right. Each token needs a full forward pass through the network, so latency grows with the length of the response, and you're limited by memory bandwidth rather than compute. Diffusion models work differently. They start from a rough, noisy draft of the whole response and refine many tokens in parallel over a small number of steps. That makes much better use of the GPU, and in practice you can get several times higher throughput and much lower time to a complete answer at comparable quality.

For voice agents specifically, that speed buys you a few things. First, the response simply feels more natural because the agent isn't hesitating. Second, you get a latency budget you can reinvest. You can use a larger, smarter model, do some reasoning, or make a tool call, like checking a database or a calendar, and still respond within the window a human expects. With a slower model you often have to choose between being fast and being smart, and diffusion helps you avoid that trade-off.

There's also a cost angle. Voice agents in customer support, scheduling, and similar settings run at huge volume, and better hardware utilization means lower cost per conversation, which matters a lot when you're deploying at scale.

Finally, the generation process gives you some extra flexibility. Because the model refines the whole output instead of committing to each token irreversibly, it can correct itself during generation and is easier to steer toward constraints, like a particular format or keeping responses short and speakable. For a real-time conversational system, that combination of speed, quality, and controllability makes diffusion a very natural fit.

r001.rationale: The response calls language-model latency a bottleneck and says slower models force a speed-versus-intelligence trade-off, but it does not specifically identify reasoning-model latency as a barrier to using reasoning models in voice agents.

r002.rationale: The response discusses lower cost per conversation at scale through better hardware utilization, but it does not identify the cost of specialized AI inference chips as a deployment barrier for reasoning models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is latency, and the slightly longer answer is latency plus the ability to fix your mistakes.

Think about what a voice agent actually has to do. Someone speaks, there's a transcription step, the model has to reason about what was said, generate a response, and then that response gets turned into speech. All of that has to happen before the pause becomes awkward, and humans are incredibly sensitive to that. In a normal conversation, the gap between one person finishing and the other starting is a couple hundred milliseconds. If your agent takes two or three seconds to start talking, it immediately feels like you're talking to a machine, no matter how good the content is.

Autoregressive language models have a fundamental problem here. They generate one token at a time, left to right, and each token depends on all the ones before it. So the time it takes to produce a response scales linearly with the length of that response. You can make the model smaller, you can do speculative decoding, you can throw more hardware at it, but you're always fighting against that sequential bottleneck.

Diffusion models work differently. Instead of producing text token by token, they start from noise, or a fully masked sequence, and refine the whole thing in parallel over a small number of steps. So you're generating many tokens at once, and the number of steps doesn't need to grow with the length of the output. In practice, that gives you something like five to ten times the throughput of a comparable autoregressive model, and for a voice agent that's the difference between a response that feels natural and one that doesn't.

The second thing, which I think people underappreciate, is that diffusion gives you a form of self-correction. In an autoregressive model, once you've committed to a token, it's there. If the model makes a bad choice early in the sentence, everything after it has to work around that mistake. With diffusion, the model is looking at the entire draft at every step, so it can revise. That matters a lot for things like structured outputs, following constraints, or making sure the response actually answers the question that was asked rather than drifting partway through.

And there's a third piece that's specific to voice. Spoken interactions are interrupted, they're messy, the user changes their mind halfway through a sentence. A model that can look at the whole context and regenerate a coherent response quickly is just a better fit for that kind of dynamic than one that's locked into a single forward pass through the text.

So when we started building Mercury at Inception, voice agents were one of the first places where customers immediately understood why this mattered. They didn't need to be convinced about the architecture. They just saw that the agent started talking faster and that it made fewer of the kinds of errors that break the illusion of a conversation.

r001.rationale: The response describes latency from the voice-agent pipeline and the sequential token generation of autoregressive models, but does not identify latency of reasoning models as a barrier.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the cost of specialized AI inference chips or high-volume deployment costs.

astra-6.text:
I think the main appeal is the potential for low latency. In a voice conversation, you want the agent to respond quickly, and generating a response one token at a time creates a sequential bottleneck. With diffusion, you can potentially generate and refine multiple tokens in parallel, giving you another way to trade off computation and response quality.

The interesting challenge is streaming. You don’t necessarily want to wait for the entire response before you start speaking, but once you’ve spoken something, you can’t revise it. So you need a way to commit to an early part of the response while continuing to refine what comes next. If we can get that balance right, diffusion could be a useful foundation for more responsive voice agents.

sol-6.1.text:
For a voice agent, latency is incredibly important. You want the conversation to feel natural, and that means the system needs to respond quickly. With an autoregressive language model, you generate one token at a time, so there’s a sequential bottleneck. Diffusion gives you a way to generate multiple tokens in parallel and potentially reduce that bottleneck.

There’s also an interesting tradeoff between speed and how much computation you spend refining an answer. You can use fewer denoising steps when you need a quick response, or more steps when the task warrants it. That doesn’t automatically make diffusion faster in every setting, but it gives us another way to design systems around the demands of a real-time conversation.
